newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. body recovers $9m lost to fraud, inefficiency.
newsitem.headline: U.N. body recovers $9m lost to fraud, inefficiency.

text.p: A U.N. watchdog unit said on Tuesday it saved or recovered nearly nine million dollars in the year ending June 30 after identifying cases of fraud or inefficiency.
The U.N. office of internal oversight services (OIOS), established in 1994 and headed by Under-Secretary-General Karl Paschke of Germany, focused on peacekeeping, humanitarian and related activities.

"Almost $9 million in savings and recoveries were realised from actions recommended by the division during this and prior periods," it said in a report. The annual U.N. regular budget totals some $1.3 billion while peacekeeping accounts for a similar sum.

A probe of the U.N. Peace Forces (UNPF) in the former Yugoslavia, now largely superseded by a NATO-led force, found they bought some 650 generators valued at $7.2 million that were not used or were sent to other U.N. missions.

"The fact that many of the contingents brought in their own generating capacity appeared not to have been considered in the planning. As a result, UNPF paid for generators not required in addition to the depreciation expense of the contingent-owned generators," the report said.
Generators also caused a headache for the U.N. Mission in Haiti (UNMIH), to which 39 were shipped but found on arrival to be incompatible with the local electrical equipment.
They had to be sent back to the U.N. logistics base in Italy, "resulting in unnecessary shipping costs of $328,000."

Also, 59 containers of expired food rations were transferred from the U.N. force in Somalia to the one in Rwanda. The rations had been found fit for consumption when inspected in 1994 but were later "stored in the blazing sun and used as a protective barrier around the offices" of the secretary-general's special representative in Somalia.
"As a result, the United Nations incurred substantial unnecessary shipping costs and port charges and had to spend an additional $40,000 to have the food destroyed."

An investigation of two senior staff of the U.N. Disengagement Observer Force (UNDOF) on the Golan Heights found that a "favored contractor, who had been supplying UNDOF with fresh food rations for the previous 12 years, had been providing poor-quality products and using United Nations trucks to smuggle import-controlled goods" into Syria.
The bidding process had been manipulated in favour of the contractor "even though his bid was $200,000 higher than the lowest acceptable bidder," the report said.

It said problems in applying regulations on subsistence allowances for U.N. peacekeepers resulted in overpayments of hundreds of thousands of dollars to staff "and the Organisation incurred significant financial loss owing to a lack of timely recovery action."

At Habitat, the Nairobi-based U.N. Centre for Human Settlements, "one staff member alone was overpaid by $150,000, having received an average monthly overpayment of approximately $2,500 over several years."

"In another case, resulting in an overpayment of $33,000 over a three-year period, a staff member was paid rental subsidy at rates applicable to a lease agreement for a New York apartment even after taking residence on another continent."

An example of problems which arise when a new U.N. body is established was the hiring of up to 15 guards for the War Crimes Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, based in The Hague, "more than half a year before the first detainee arrived and even before the construction of the detention facilities was completed."
